slides.title: Introduction
slides.body:
Introduction
ALOHA : The First Random Access Protocol
Multiple Devices Transmitting
Devices Transmitting at the same time
ALOHA is a random access protocol that allows multiple devices to share a communication channel by transmitting whenever they have data
If two devices transmit at the same time, a collision occurs, and data must be retransmitted

slides.title: Importance
slides.body:
Importance
ALOHA : The First Random Access Protocol
Multiple devices needed to share a single wireless channel
No coordination mechanism existed in early systems
Goal: Allow simple and independent transmission

2. Slotted ALOHA
Time is divided into equal slots. A device can only begin transmitting at the start of a slot.
Reduces the collision window by half compared to Pure ALOHA.
Maximum efficiency: 36.8%  →  roughly double the throughput of Pure ALOHA

slides.title: Introduction
slides.body:
Introduction
CSMA
CSMA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access) is a network protocol in which a device first checks (listens) whether the communication channel is free before transmitting data. It improves ALOHA by ensuring that a device transmits only when the channel is idle; otherwise, it waits
Listening for Channel
Channel Idle
Transmitting Data

slides.title: How CSMA Works?
slides.body:
How CSMA Works?
CSMA
Device wants to transmit → listens to the channel
If the channel is idle → transmit
If the channel is busy → wait

slides.title: Introduction
slides.body:
Introduction
Controlled Access Protocols
Controlled access protocols ensure that only one device transmits at a time, eliminating collisions completely by requiring explicit permission before sending data

slides.title: Reservation Time is divided into fixed-length frames, each containing a reservat
slides.body:
Reservation Time is divided into fixed-length frames, each containing a reservation interval followed by data slots
Each station reserves a slot in the reservation interval before transmitting
If a station wants to send → it sets its bit in the reservation interval
1. Reservation
Controlled Access Protocols

slides.body:

slides.title: A primary (central controller) manages all communication
slides.body:
A primary (central controller) manages all communication
Primary stations poll each device one by one: “Do you have data to send?”
If a device has data → it transmits
If not → controller immediately moves to the next device
Process repeats in a cycle
2. Polling

slides.title: 3. Token Passing
slides.body:
3. Token Passing
Controlled Access Protocols
A token (control frame) circulates in a logical ring
Only the device holding the token can transmit
After transmission (or if no data), token is passed to next device
Used in Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) and FDDI networks

slides.body:
Key Properties
3. Token Passing
No collisions
Guaranteed access for all stations
Predictable communication delay (latency)

Introduction
Channelization
Channelization divides a shared channel into smaller logical parts, so multiple devices can transmit without collisions

slides.title: Deep Dive
slides.body:
Deep Dive
1. FDMA – Frequency Division Multiple Access
Total bandwidth is divided into frequency bands (channels)
Each device gets a dedicated frequency
All devices transmit simultaneously
Used in: 1G cellular networks, Radio broadcasting

slides.title: Key Points
slides.body:
Key Points
1. FDMA – Frequency Division Multiple Access
Guard bands prevent overlap between frequencies
Unused frequency → wasted bandwidth
